new_card.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
new_card.q: In the wake of the 'Ned-Leaks' scandals it becomes known that the Netherlands is a tax haven and that its tax-avoidance schemes distort competition in the EU. Commission President Peter Niederknaaken was previously Minister of Finance of the Netherlands and is coming under fire because of the Ned-Leaks scandals. Does the European Parliament have the power to remove Commission President Niederknaaken? (2 points)
new_card.a:
Short answer: No. The European Parliament cannot remove the Commission President on his own; it can only bring down the whole Commission by a motion of censure (Art 17(8) TEU, Art 234 TFEU).
• Rule: the Commission as a body is responsible to the Parliament (Art 17(8) TEU). A motion of censure may be voted on no earlier than three days after it is tabled, and only by open vote. It needs a two-thirds majority of the votes cast, representing a majority of the component Members (Art 234 TFEU; currently 361 of 720).
• Consequence: if the motion is carried, the members of the Commission, including the President, must resign as a body, and the High Representative resigns from the duties he or she carries out in the Commission. They continue to deal with current business until they are replaced, and the new Commission serves only the rest of the term (Art 234(2) TFEU). There is no censure of the President or of a single Commissioner alone.
• Application: the EP can reach Niederknaaken only by censuring the entire college. Otherwise it has only political control (Art 14(1) TEU): resolutions, questions (Art 230 TFEU) and a committee of inquiry (Art 226 TFEU). He may resign voluntarily (Art 246 TFEU). Compulsory retirement, for serious misconduct or for no longer fulfilling the conditions of office, is ordered by the Court of Justice only on application of the Council or the Commission, never the EP (Art 247 TFEU).
• Conclusion: the EP has no power to remove Niederknaaken individually.
Codex: Art 14(1), 17(7)–(8) TEU; Art 226, 230, 234, 246, 247 TFEU.

new_card.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
new_card.q: In connection with the Ned-Leaks tax-avoidance scandals, an EU legal act is issued in the form of a regulation. Can it nevertheless be transposed into national law? (2 points)
new_card.a:
Short answer: No. A regulation is directly applicable in all Member States (Art 288(2) TFEU), so it needs no transposition and must not be transposed; only accompanying implementing measures are allowed.
• Rule: a regulation has general application, is binding in its entirety and is directly applicable in all Member States (Art 288(2) TFEU). It becomes part of national law automatically once it is published in the Official Journal and enters into force (Art 297 TFEU). A directive, by contrast, must be transposed (Art 288(3) TFEU).
• Ban on transposition: Member States may not adopt measures that conceal the Union nature of the rule, alter its content or delay its application. Such measures would endanger its simultaneous and uniform application and the Court's jurisdiction under Art 267 TFEU (Variola, 34/73; Commission v Italy, 39/72).
• Limits: national implementing measures are allowed, and even required, where the regulation calls for them or leaves gaps, e.g. designating the competent authorities or laying down penalties (Art 291(1) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU). Repeating some provisions is tolerated only to keep a complex national regime coherent and comprehensible (Commission v Italy, 272/83).
• Conclusion: the regulation applies as it stands. Re-enacting it as a national statute would itself infringe EU law (Art 258 TFEU).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 258, 267, 288(2)–(3), 291(1), 297 TFEU · Variola (34/73), Commission v Italy (39/72), Commission v Italy (272/83).

subquestions.label: Case 1 Q5

new_card.q: How does the Court of Justice justify the primacy of EU law over national law? (3 points)
new_card.a:
Short answer: No Treaty article lays down primacy; the Court derives it from the nature of EU law as an autonomous legal order to which the Member States transferred sovereign rights, and from the need to apply that law uniformly and effectively (Costa v ENEL, 6/64).
• Autonomous legal order: unlike ordinary international treaties, the Treaty created its own legal system. On entry into force it became an integral part of the Member States' legal systems, which their courts are bound to apply (Costa, building on the 'new legal order' of Van Gend en Loos, 26/62).
• Transfer of sovereignty: the Member States created a Community of unlimited duration with its own institutions, personality and real powers. In doing so they limited their sovereign rights and created a body of law that binds their nationals and themselves. The argument is from consent.
• Reciprocity and uniformity: a state cannot give precedence to a unilateral, later national measure over a legal order accepted on the basis of reciprocity. The executive force of EU law cannot vary from state to state without jeopardising the Treaty's objectives and causing discrimination prohibited by Art 18 TFEU.
• Textual support: the duty of sincere cooperation (then Art 5 EEC, now Art 4(3) TEU; not Art 3(3) TEU, which lists the Union's objectives) and the direct applicability of regulations (Art 288(2) TFEU), which would be meaningless if later national law could override them. The Treaty's special derogation procedures would also lose their purpose.
• Later case law: effectiveness requires every national court to set aside conflicting national law (Simmenthal, 106/77). Primacy also covers national constitutional law (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70). The equality of the Member States before the Treaties (Art 4(2) TEU) is possible only if they cannot rely on national rules against EU law (RS, C-430/21). Declaration 17 merely recalls this case law.
Codex: Art 4(2)–(3) TEU; Art 18, 288(2) TFEU; Declaration 17 · Costa v ENEL (6/64), Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Simmenthal (106/77), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70), RS (C-430/21).

subquestions.label: Case 1 Q7

new_card.q: What is an ultra vires act? (2 points)
new_card.a:
Short answer: An ultra vires act is an act of a Union institution, body, office or agency adopted beyond the competences the Treaties confer on the Union or on that institution; under EU law only the Court of Justice of the European Union can declare it invalid, although some national constitutional courts claim a residual right to treat it as inapplicable.
• Rule: under the principle of conferral the Union acts only within the competences conferred on it by the Member States (Art 5(1)–(2) TEU). Competences not conferred remain with the Member States (Art 4(1) TEU). Each institution acts only within the powers conferred on it (Art 13(2) TEU). An act beyond these limits lacks a legal basis.
• EU perspective: such an act is unlawful but presumed valid until the CJEU annuls it for lack of competence (Art 263(2) TFEU), declares it invalid on a preliminary reference (Art 267 TFEU) or holds it inapplicable on a plea of illegality (Art 277 TFEU). National courts cannot declare EU acts invalid (Foto-Frost, 314/85).
• National perspective: the German Federal Constitutional Court holds that an act outside the integration programme approved by the national parliament does not apply in Germany (Maastricht 1993, Lisbon 2009). Since Honeywell (2010) it applies this only after a preliminary reference and only where the excess is manifest and structurally significant. It first did so in PSPP (2020).
• Distinguish: a Member State's breach of EU law is an infringement (Art 4(3) TEU, Art 258 TFEU), not an ultra vires act.
Codex: Art 4(1), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU; Art 263(2), 267, 277 TFEU · Foto-Frost (314/85); BVerfG Maastricht, Honeywell, PSPP (not in codex).
